name: Semiconductor Fab

claims.claim_text: A wafer fab that produces commodity chips costs billions of dollars to build; the disparity between a multi-billion-dollar plant and a twenty-cent part is what forces semiconductor manufacturing into extreme volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a reason why it costs, you know, $5 billion to make a fab plant
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cultural Differences

claims.claim_text: The barrier to home or small-scale chip fabrication is the number and complexity of the chemical process steps rather than the patterning itself; the same step count is why production fab houses cost hundreds of millions of dollars at minimum.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why these fab houses that make these chips cost hundreds of millions of dollars at a minimum
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Military Electronics and The Free Eagle (Freagle) Campaign

claims.claim_text: As the cost of building a fab rose, fewer companies could afford one, which drove both industry consolidation and the growth of dedicated foundries such as TSMC.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost to build a fab has gotten so high that, you know, there aren't very many people who can afford to do it anymore
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: A fully depreciated older fab, for example a 500 nm line, can still be commercially interesting: the capital is written off and process variation at that geometry is not a significant constraint, so useful parts can be built cheaply.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of these old 500 nanometer fabs and realize they could build some way cool parts because the fab is entirely depreciated
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Around 2012 the quoted cost to convert an existing 300 mm line to 450 mm wafers was about $2 billion, against roughly $5 billion for a complete new full-size fab, making conversion and greenfield construction economically comparable.
claims.quote_verbatim: No, it's saying $2 billion to upgrade from 300 millimeter up to 450 millimeter.
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: Wafer-size conversions are done in stages, routing some wafer types to converted tools and others to the old tools, because fabs avoid downtime wherever possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's very little in the way of downtime in fabs if they can help it.
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: Because each process step takes a long time regardless of how many die are on the wafer, fab economics push toward maximising the number of chips per wafer.
claims.quote_verbatim: you gotta try and maximize the chips per wafer
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: The capital in a fab is in the process equipment, so the operating goal is to keep those tools running at 90 to 95 percent utilisation and push through the maximum number of wafers.
claims.quote_verbatim: So making sure those things are used 90%, 95% so that they're always running
claims.episode_title: Cores, Digikey, Electronic Design - The Commercial Competitor Commencement

claims.claim_text: Reaching a new process node first confers pricing power: the leader can charge what it likes for parts nobody else can make until competitors catch up, which is how a $5-10 billion fab investment is recovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: If Intel gets to 10 nanometers first and it takes them $10 billion to build a new fab
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: A new leading-edge fab may not turn a profit for something like five years after it is built.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they're not even going to break a profit for, what, like five years on a fab?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: TSMC's first 450 mm fab, succeeding its 300 mm (12-inch) plants, was quoted at eight to ten billion dollars, a figure treated as the going rate for a modern fab at the time.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're actually building their first 450 millimeter fab versus 300 millimeter fab, which is 12 inches. And they said eight to 10 billion dollars
claims.episode_title: Bonkers Birthday Badinage

claims.claim_text: With a new leading-edge fab costing on the order of ten to fifteen billion dollars, new entrants cannot build one, so access to an existing fab is the only route to silicon and the fabless model becomes the default industry structure.
claims.quote_verbatim: to build a new fab costs, you know, 10, 15 billion dollars minimum
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mergers and Acquiescence

claims.claim_text: The compensating benefit of the fabless model is that a small startup with a good analog layout engineer gets access to the same fabs and design tools as a company with its own ten-billion-dollar fab.
claims.quote_verbatim: has access to the same tools as, you know, a 10 billion dollar fab company
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mergers and Acquiescence

claims.claim_text: Starting a semiconductor company that owns its own fab is not viable for a startup: the up-front cost is around two billion dollars, so new companies begin fabless.
claims.quote_verbatim: It would cost $2 billion right up front.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: No startup can raise the roughly one billion dollars needed to buy a fab, which is why chip companies begin by farming production out, in the same way a new board maker uses an assembly house before buying its own SMT line.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's no way you can get the investment capital to, you know, a billion dollars to buy your own fab.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: A company with its own fab is capacity-limited to whatever that fab starts, for example 20,000 wafers a week, and must ration allocation among customers; farming out to a foundry removes that fixed ceiling.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can start, you know, 20,000 wafers a week.
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: Fab ownership is a low-margin business, and is only absorbable by companies large enough to treat a couple of billion dollars as incidental.
claims.quote_verbatim: Low profit margins and everything else. Like, you want to get rich, do not buy a chip fab.
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: Because a decent fab represents a five-to-ten-billion-dollar investment, the operator runs it for twenty or thirty years rather than closing it; once the plant is paid off many times over, the chips coming out of it get progressively cheaper.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've paid off that fab 10 times over. So the chips just get cheaper and cheaper
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Fab economics work as a reverse annuity: a multi-billion-dollar loan buys the building and machinery, and every wafer sold thereafter pays down that machinery, which is why prices fall as a process moves to trailing edge.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get your massive loan for billions of dollars and then you build your fab and buy all your machinery. And then you're basically selling wafers until you've paid off all the machines.
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: A trailing-edge line such as a 180 nm fab, roughly a dozen generations behind the leading edge, is kept running because the equipment is already paid for; the resulting excess capacity can be sold cheaply to new kinds of customer even though its marginal cost is not zero.
claims.quote_verbatim: they still keep it running because there's, because it's already been paid for. And so now that becomes excess capacity.
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: A foundry is a fab that sells its process capability to outside customers: TSMC is the canonical example, Samsung has foundry capability alongside its own products, GlobalFoundries was spun out of AMD, and SkyWater runs open-source process offerings.
claims.quote_verbatim: TSMC is a, is a foundry where they will, you show up, you buy their, you know, capability
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: GlobalFoundries exists because AMD split its fabs out of the design company, a separation repeatedly predicted for other integrated device manufacturers.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically global foundries is what AMD did, which I think Intel will eventually do. They split out the fab
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: IBM exited manufacturing by paying GlobalFoundries to take its fabs, an inversion of the normal sale that shows how a fab can be a net liability.
claims.quote_verbatim: we saw IBM do their spinoff. They just paid global foundries a bunch of money to take their fabs off their hands
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: Being fabless does not make the playing field level: the largest FPGA vendors keep process-technology staff who work directly with TSMC and UMC on custom processes, and may hold exclusive access to a new process for its first year.
claims.quote_verbatim: Companies like Xilinx and Ultera have process technology people on staff
claims.speaker: Philip Freidin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: When two competitors use the same foundry and the same node, the process is no longer a differentiator; the only remaining variable in getting a chip out is design and verification speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no variable between, you know, getting a chip out the door other than how fast you can verify something
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: A leading-edge foundry serves FPGAs, custom ASICs and large SoCs, not analog parts; a large customer will put a design out to bid across TSMC, Samsung and Intel and choose on price and availability.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like bleeding edge foundry
claims.episode_title: A literal trainwreck

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments continued to run its own fabs and treated in-house capacity as a competitive position of strength rather than a cost to be shed.
claims.quote_verbatim: TI still run their own fabs
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Analog vendors split on manufacturing strategy: Linear Technology continued to run its own fabs while Analog Devices used a mixture of its own fabs and the TSMC foundry model.
claims.quote_verbatim: LT still operates their own fabs. As far as I know, ADI does joint.
claims.episode_title: Mergers and Acquiescence

claims.claim_text: Consolidating many products onto shared foundry capacity concentrates risk: when one fab goes down, a large fraction of a designer's parts become unavailable at once, an effect visible during the COVID-era shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like one fab goes down, and half your parts are unavailable.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Divesting process technology also gives up tribal knowledge and the incremental innovations that come from being on the shop floor, a cost that does not appear on the financial case for going fabless.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you give it up, you give up a ton of like tribal knowledge
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: For a microcontroller vendor, moving to a foundry may be rational, but for an analog company the process is the differentiation and there is little else left to compete on.
claims.quote_verbatim: But for the analog people, it's like, guys, that's all you have left.
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: Publishing FPGA architecture and bitstream information does not give away the business, because the defensible know-how is in manufacturing at scale with good quality, reliability and yield, plus test tricks, which are held as trade secrets rather than patents.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not how you would actually manufacture it at scale with good quality, reliability, good yields
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Process development is a foundry's core intellectual property, so process design kits are traditionally released only under NDA even though designers need them to target the process at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: So traditionally you have to sign an NDA, then you get given the PDK.
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Google's open-source PDK programme paired an openly published process design kit with free wafer fabrication at 130 nm, on the condition that the design itself be open source.
claims.quote_verbatim: Google is offering free semiconductor wafer fabbing for 130 nanometer technology. Free for open source chips.
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: Holding a full process node lead over competitors, as with a 20 nm line while others were a node behind, is bought with capital rather than won on design.
claims.quote_verbatim: Intel is on 20 nanometers right now, which is an entire process node
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: The move to FinFET and other three-dimensional transistor structures was part of how the leading-edge logic process kept its performance advantage.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're already into FinFets and all the other crazy 3D, 3D based transistors
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: TSMC's 16 nm FinFET process, qualified as the successor to 22 nm, ran at a core voltage of 0.55 V.
claims.quote_verbatim: The core voltage is 0.55 volts.
claims.episode_title: Robots are coming - Ominous Operational Overhaul

claims.claim_text: Below the FinFET nodes the printed dimensions are smaller than the deep-UV wavelength can resolve, so a single layer is decomposed into several coarser patterns that are exposed on top of one another; this multiple patterning is what buys the fine resolution.
claims.quote_verbatim: so what they do is that they do this thing called multiple patterning
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: Multiple patterning removes layout freedom: devices can no longer be placed in arbitrary orientations, and everything on a patterned layer must run in the same direction, which is one of many rules that make modern DRC decks enormous.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything has to be the same direction
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: Only two or three companies in the world can run 5 nm and 3 nm class CMOS processes, and the rising cost of each node is the counterpart to the flattening of Moore's law.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's only maybe two or three semiconductor companies now in the world that can do these five three kind of nanometer process
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: High-speed and RF parts are typically not built in leading-edge CMOS but in silicon-germanium BiCMOS, a hybrid process in which SiGe bipolar devices give higher breakdown voltage and power handling while an ordinary, non-advanced CMOS sits on the same wafer as a helper device.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's called a silicon germanium by cmos process but they put them all on the same wafer
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: EUV patterning machines cost over a hundred million dollars each and are what a 3 nm process requires, so a plant budgeted at $1.2 billion cannot be a leading-edge line and must be built on older, cheaper equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're like a hundred, a hundred plus million dollars these days, you know, EUV machines
claims.episode_title: Thousands Of Dependencies

claims.claim_text: Feature size is not uniform across a die: the gate is the tightest dimension, so selective patterning puts gates through the newest and most accurate exposure equipment while larger features are printed on older tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fanciest equipment in the fab is used for the tightest tolerance
claims.episode_title: Good Energy Citizen

claims.claim_text: At the leading edge of around 7 nm, transmission electron microscope cross-sections of the transistors are on the order of 50 to 70 atoms wide.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're literally 50 atoms wide, you know, it's nuts, 50, 70 atoms
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Metal-gate MOSFET processes were abandoned in the 1970s and returned decades later, because polysilicon and silicides stop working at very small feature sizes and refractory metals had to be revived.
claims.quote_verbatim: MetalGate on MOSFETs was abandoned in the 70s because of some limitations
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Process techniques abandoned in the 1960s and 1970s were often dropped for throughput reasons rather than because they did not work, so older process literature is a useful source for anyone recreating a process at low volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: Things that were tried were abandoned because, at the time, you know, they couldn't run 100,000 wafers per hour through a fab with that technology.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Older fabs ran much of their etch and ash equipment essentially open to the air; modern equivalents are high-vacuum chambers, and that vacuum is what makes the fine geometries achievable.
claims.quote_verbatim: these days, they're like vacuum chambers, and, you know, you have to have, like, really high vacuum to get all these good geometries
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: There are physical reasons not to move analog parts to small nodes: leakage at 16 nm demands elaborate compensation, and a trench power FET needs geometries orders of magnitude larger, so demands that carmakers move off older processes miss the point.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like tons and tons of leakage at 16 nanometers
claims.episode_title: Occam's Engineering Razor

claims.claim_text: A further practical block on analog at small nodes is tooling rather than physics: the analog design package for those processes is not made available.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't get access to the analog design package for the lower stuff
claims.episode_title: Occam's Engineering Razor

claims.claim_text: A switching power supply is not going to be built on a leading-edge node; even a very advanced one is made on a 90 nm or 45 nm process, so leading-edge fab investment does not address shortages of that class of part.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're going to build it on a 90 nanometer or 45 nanometer process
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Same Wavelength

claims.claim_text: Useful products can still be built on an old node such as 180 nm when the design is not constrained by die size or power budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could do, you know, 180 nanometers, still do some cool stuff
claims.episode_title: DIP projects, OSHW & Trade Booths - Demonstrative DIP Dacrygelosis

claims.claim_text: Improving fab technology let more current be carried on the die itself, which is why switching regulators migrated from controllers with external FETs to converters with the FETs integrated, removing parts from the bill of materials and simplifying the design equations.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can, a lot of them can handle more current on the actual die, and so they pull the FET internal and they become converters
claims.episode_title: Part Choice Triathlon

claims.claim_text: CMOS image sensors are made on a comparatively standard semiconductor process and allow control logic and ADCs to be integrated on the same die, whereas CCD sensors need a different, specialised process.
claims.quote_verbatim: I believe CMOS sensors are a much more standard process that can be done on normal semiconductor equipment
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Silicon carbide cannot be pulled from a melt the way silicon or sapphire can, because it does not melt, so SiC boules must be grown by a different method entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: the silicon carbide doesn't melt, so you can't pull it from a liquid like you can with silicon or sapphire
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: One-centimetre wafers are adequate for laboratory research on a new semiconductor material, but a real manufacturing process needs four- or six-inch wafers, and the driver is cost per die rather than yield alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: But to get to a real manufacturing process, you need, you know, four inch, six inch.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Four-inch wafer production is no longer economical except for very high-value parts, such as a 24-bit converter selling for $25; for an ordinary chip selling between fifty cents and three dollars even six-inch wafers are not viable.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no economical point anymore to be running four-inch wafers
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Traditional analog makers that once ran their own fabs divested them because chartering wafers from a large foundry became cheaper than operating a small, old line.
claims.quote_verbatim: at one point they used to have their own fabs, but they have gotten rid of their fabs because it is cheaper for them to just charter wafers
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: IGZO, an indium gallium zinc oxide process, was used for MEMS-adjacent research work, run in a low-grade R&D fab rather than a production line.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was using a, a, a process called Igzo and, um, it's indium gallium zinc
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Joe Bamberg

claims.claim_text: Die size drives yield sharply: a die a centimetre on a side must yield well or the process is out of control, because defect density that is tolerable on a small die is fatal on a large one.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you aren't yielding well on a square centimeter die, then your fab is out of control.
claims.speaker: Philip Freidin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Mask-set cost at the most current process technology exceeded ten million dollars, and that cost rising with each node shrink is what steadily narrows the range of applications where an ASIC beats an FPGA.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting over $10 million for a mask set
claims.speaker: Philip Freidin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: A multi-project shuttle run gives low-volume silicon for a couple of hundred thousand dollars, but moving the same 20 nm design into volume production costs about three million dollars more.
claims.quote_verbatim: shuttle basically low volume production at, uh, at a couple hundred thousand dollars
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Commercial tape-outs justify extensive simulation because a mistake wastes the mask and run cost, quoted at around ten thousand dollars for a small shuttle slot.
claims.quote_verbatim: they usually want to simulate a bunch because they don't want to waste the $10,000
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: A cheap-respin service commoditises the process by fixing the transistor array and customising only the metallisation layers over the top, which is what makes a few-hundred-dollar prototype possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: they basically do the metalized layer over top of a fixed set of semiconductors
claims.episode_title: Cheap Respins And A Time Machine - Multiscience Mercenary Marketplace

claims.claim_text: The first run of a 400 V, one-ohm power MOSFET came back at two ohms because one drawn dimension between openings was 10 microns instead of 15; a single geometry error on the mask meant discarding the whole design and starting again.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of a 15 micron separation between these two openings, I'd made 10 microns
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: A small company taping out a mixed-signal chip chose a fab running an older process specifically because that was the tape-out it could afford.
claims.quote_verbatim: the model at that time was to find a, a fab that had some, a bit of an old process, uh, so that we could afford to, to do tape out in it
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jørgen Jakobsen

claims.claim_text: Surface states are the dominant obstacle for anyone fabricating semiconductors by hand, particularly with point-contact devices; the first transistor only worked once the contact tip was immersed in an electrolyte.
claims.quote_verbatim: surface states are like the bane of the existence of people trying to make semiconductors
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Ghost of Keyzermas Past

claims.claim_text: Etch chambers foul as wafers are processed, so the quartz kits inside them must periodically be swapped out; the chamber then has to be pumped down, tested and verified before it can return to production.
claims.quote_verbatim: eventually, wafers dirty up the chambers, right? And eventually, you have to switch out these quartz kits that are inside of them
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: Because a fab line is designed for full utilisation, a single tool going down costs both the lost capacity and a growing queue of work in progress behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's designed for 100% utilization
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: An unplanned power loss in a plasma etch chamber drops the material suspended above the wafer straight onto it, scrapping large numbers of wafers in progress.
claims.quote_verbatim: All that stuff that's floating drops, drops a whole bunch of crap. And yeah, you scrap a lot of wafers.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: Cleanroom garments are a consumable-like resource: after wear they go to a dirty bin, are laundered to remove particulates and re-wrapped, and a missing size means working in ill-fitting kit.
claims.quote_verbatim: they would go take them out, clean them, and get all the particulates off, and then re-wrap them up
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: A wafer's route through the fab is a supply chain in miniature: photolithography exposes the wafer, it is rinsed, then it moves to dry etch or ash, and a fault at any station backs up everything behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're exposing a wafer and then they rinse it and then it's supposed to go to dry ash
claims.episode_title: Lowest Common Denominator Design

claims.claim_text: Modern chip fabs are largely fully automated, with wafers moving through the line and tested chips emerging with little manual handling.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of these chip fabs are all, like, full auto these days
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: A fab building is roughly ten storeys tall, of which the fab floor itself may be three storeys of open internal space; below it sit hollow service floors carrying pumps, piping, water, chemicals and power for the tools above.
claims.quote_verbatim: the actual fab itself might be three stories open internally, but then usually it's a hollow floor as well
claims.episode_title: Good Energy Citizen

claims.claim_text: Fab shells avoid internal pillars, so roof trusses span the full width of the building to leave the process floor clear.
claims.quote_verbatim: the truss spans are often the entire width of the building
claims.episode_title: Good Energy Citizen

claims.claim_text: Large fabs are built as stacked structures, with one fab floor on top of another, to multiply capacity on a single site.
claims.quote_verbatim: they usually build them two stories high
claims.episode_title: IoT Degree

claims.claim_text: The hard part of building a fab is the facility rather than the shell: the sub-basements, piping and utility logistics needed to feed the tools, including very large volumes of water.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the logistics of just getting piping in
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: Fabs consume very large quantities of water, which is a first-order siting constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: fabs need water. They need lots of water.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: Water supply is a real production risk, not a theoretical one: Taiwan had to reduce chip output during a water shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: Taiwan had to reduce its chip output because of a water shortage
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: Ground stability is a fab siting criterion because lithography alignment cannot tolerate vibration; porous limestone bedrock that absorbs vibration and low seismic activity are advantages when choosing a site.
claims.quote_verbatim: the rock is really porous and it kind of absorbs vibration
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Analog Devices built a fab in Ireland on the strength of tax incentives plus the ease of flying wafers in and finished chips out, and the resulting cluster attracted further semiconductor investment and graduates to the region.
claims.quote_verbatim: ADI came along and they built a fab here for that exact reason. It's easy to fly in wafers and easy to fly out chips.
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Fab scale is hard to picture from the outside: one plant measured about nine football fields across, made up of nine bays side by side.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fab that I worked in was nine football fields long
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: Fabs are heavily chemical-dependent, so a supporting ecosystem of chemical suppliers and service companies grows up around an established fab site.
claims.quote_verbatim: fabs are incredibly chemical dependent
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: US fab work is geographically concentrated - Oregon, Boise, Arizona, Richardson in Texas, Austin, and the Albany and East Fishkill area of New York - and process work on the floor cannot be done remotely, so the industry constrains where its engineers can live.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't really telecommute in the chip industry unless you have maybe design in the chip or something
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: Siting a fab away from an existing cluster creates a staffing problem, since the nearest comparable fab may be many hours' drive away and experienced process staff have to be recruited or developed from scratch.
claims.quote_verbatim: the closest fabs to there are in Albany, which is, you know, another nine hours away by car
claims.episode_title: A literal trainwreck

claims.claim_text: The quoted internal cycle for a chip order is roughly thirty days to make the silicon, then dicing, packaging and test, and then a wait to be slotted into the fab's schedule; no customer gets a dedicated line.
claims.quote_verbatim: It takes 30 days to make the silicon. And then you got to cut it up.
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: A dominant customer can demand the entire output of a production line for a new product, which pushes every other customer down the queue and is a recurring cause of apparent shortages.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll demand that you give them all of your stock, you know, everything that comes off the production line
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Loopback

claims.claim_text: The post-2008 shortage came from the whole chain stopping at once: orders were cancelled, backlogs sold off, workers laid off, and a fab cannot be restarted quickly once it has been shut down.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can't start a fab back up
claims.episode_title: Loopback

claims.claim_text: Lead times of 30 to 40 weeks were seen after fab shutdowns, which is why high-volume designs are expected to carry second and third sources for critical parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you hear lead times, which are, you know, how long it takes to get a part. And they're still way out there, you know, 30 weeks, 40 weeks
claims.episode_title: Girl Power

claims.claim_text: When a foundry is congested, every customer of that foundry sees the same lead times, so which fab a vendor uses becomes a supply consideration for the designer choosing between otherwise similar parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can tell who's using like TSMC as well because it's so clogged up there that like everybody has the same the same lead times
claims.episode_title: A++++++ Will Buy Again

claims.claim_text: Complex parts such as large FPGAs are often made to order: the distributor passes the order to the semiconductor fab and the process takes about six months, during which the rest of the bill of materials accumulates at the assembler as tied-up cash.
claims.quote_verbatim: then it takes six months to make them because it's some really complex process tech
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Silicon parts are largely not interchangeable during a shortage, unlike passive components where many equivalents exist in the same footprint, so a shortage of one switching regulator cannot be designed around cheaply.
claims.quote_verbatim: I posit that many silicon parts are not interchangeable
claims.episode_title: Chip Shortage Denier

claims.claim_text: Restarting mothballed fabs is not a fast route to capacity, because the capital equipment is sold off when a fab is shut down and what remains is essentially an empty building.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're just buildings at this point that they sold out all the equipment
claims.episode_title: Chip Shortage Denier

claims.claim_text: Fabs periodically retire process nodes, and the customer's option is a last-time buy: the fab announces a final run and the buyer orders enough parts, potentially a million, to cover the remaining product life.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fab just went, no, we don't have this process node anymore. Final run.
claims.episode_title: Fan Fanboys

claims.claim_text: When a semiconductor vendor changes a part's fab or process node, it issues a product change notification that propagates through distributors to anyone who has bought the part, so behaviour and specifications can shift on an otherwise unchanged part number.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will release a design change note
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Boat Anchor Warehouse

claims.claim_text: The same ordered part can come from any of several manufacturing plants worldwide and the buyer usually does not know which, because wafer fabrication and packaging happen in different places.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you order a chip, it can come from any one of five different manufacturing plants around the world
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: The industry is split by task and geography: the fab produces the wafer, which is then shipped to another country for packaging and elsewhere again for die bonding and test, and no existing factory does the whole sequence on one site.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fab does the silicon wafer and then they export them to Malaysia to get them packaged
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyper Growth and OpenClaw Interns

claims.claim_text: In wafer-level chip-scale packaging the finished wafer is not diced at the fab: it goes to a packaging fab where polymer insulator, vias and a couple of copper redistribution layers are added to route the die pads out to solder balls placed directly on the wafer, and only then is it cut into chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: you take a whole wafer and then you go to a packaging fab
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Incoming wafers are around 500 microns thick or more and are usually ground down so that the finished chips end up a few hundred microns thick.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's probably 500 microns or thicker and usually they grind them down so the final chips are probably a few hundred microns
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller vendor's fab can hold several generations of technology in production at once: EPROM, EEPROM and Flash processes all continue to run, supporting thousands of part variants.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the EEPROM technology still runs in our fab
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: Switching between those processes is a scheduling matter rather than a fab conversion: different mask sets can be started on consecutive days, or all of them on the same day, because the fab holds enough equipment to run the processes in parallel.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is enough equipment with the fab to really make all those parts in parallel.
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: Buying semiconductor capacity is unlike commissioning a specialised module: at a fab the customer is given a slot on existing equipment, whereas a specialised supplier may build production lines and even buildings to support one customer's product.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like semiconductor fabs, you're just getting a slot somewhere at a fab and, you know, it's probably using existing equipment.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Wait, why is Jeff glowing?

claims.claim_text: Burr-Brown ran its own four-inch wafer fab in Tucson and it was shut down after acquisition because a four-inch line was already becoming obsolete and the company could not fund a large modern fab.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was a four-inch wafer fab. And really, by the time we were acquired, it was obsolete or becoming obsolete.
claims.speaker: Art Kay
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Art Kay

claims.claim_text: Fab capacity moves between countries only over decades; obsolete plants are typically neither upgraded nor relocated but left to run down and become brownfield sites.
claims.quote_verbatim: because it takes many decades for fab plants to move out of countries and spread elsewhere in the world
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: DIP projects, OSHW & Trade Booths - Demonstrative DIP Dacrygelosis

claims.claim_text: The United States committed about $37 billion to boosting domestic chip manufacturing at a time when a single new plant cost roughly $15 billion, so the programme could fund only a small number of plants.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, they're putting 37 billion into it. And well, a new plant costs like 15 billion or something.
claims.episode_title: Recalling Recalls

claims.claim_text: Once CHIPS Act funding was actually in the pipeline, the announced new fabs were expected to take about two to three years or more before they were running, raising the possibility of a chip glut at the far end of a shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: there will be apparently new chip fabs in about two to three years
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: Roughly forty billion dollars of CHIPS Act money had been distributed by the United States as the programme began paying out.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like 40 billion that's been distributed by the US so far
claims.episode_title: Good Energy Citizen

claims.claim_text: Microchip examined the CHIPS Act terms, judged them golden handcuffs, and declined the funding; several other announced fab projects were scaled back for the same reason.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was golden handcuffs
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Voltage, Vibes, and VOCs

claims.claim_text: Foreign fab construction in the United States is driven substantially by politics, tax breaks and onshoring policy rather than by manufacturing logic alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's politics and it's tax breaks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Two Person Rule

claims.claim_text: A state-backed fab startup in China consumed billions of dollars over roughly five years and produced nothing, having failed to secure either the staff or the continued funding needed; spinning up a fab is a many-year undertaking.
claims.quote_verbatim: they already put, I think billions into it and they've got nothing to show for it after like five years
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: Fab capacity is limited by the machine builders as well as by the fabs: the tools are hugely complex and getting the machines that make chips is harder than getting chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: you think it's hard to get chips, try and get the machines to make chips
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: Fab construction has a natural time limit that capital cannot compress; the industry's answer to demands for more capacity during the shortage was that new plants take about six years to build.
claims.quote_verbatim: come back to us in six years when we, when we built it
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Production fab chemistry is chosen for throughput, using the strongest practical acid concentration to push hundreds of thousands of wafers through; a home process can substitute far milder chemistry, such as a rust and stain remover, and simply wait twenty minutes for an oxide etch.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're going to use the strongest acid with the strongest concentration possible
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: A garage semiconductor process can be assembled from eBay and Amazon: wafers, chemicals, general lab supplies and a furnace, with prior conversations with industry practitioners used to establish which chemicals and safety measures were needed.
claims.quote_verbatim: going on eBay and going on Amazon, ordering some wafers, ordering all the chemicals I can get my hands on
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Peter Van Zant's Microchip Fabrication, around 400 pages and free of heavy mathematics, is a usable single-volume introduction covering the whole sequence of chip manufacturing steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's by a guy named Peter Van Zandt
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: A home fabricator has to write their own design rules: a .tech file for Magic VLSI encoding minimum and maximum spacings, layer thicknesses and MOSFET characteristics lets the layout tool enforce what the garage process can actually resolve.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's all the design rules about maximum and minimum spacing between this and that layer thicknesses
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Owning the process changes the design economics: a simple three-transistor circuit can be checked by inspection and a mistaken mask simply remade, whereas a commercial tape-out must be simulated exhaustively because the run cannot be repeated cheaply.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I go to make something in my garage and oops, I didn't get the mask quite right
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Home semiconductor fabrication draws on several disciplines in sequence: device physics first, then the chemistry of the process steps, then optics once a lithography setup is being built.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I moved on to setting up my lithography setup, you learn about optics
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Used semiconductor process equipment is cheap at older geometries: a used sputtering machine runs roughly $800 to $1,000, and equipping a one-micron line is affordable because that is 1980s technology.
claims.quote_verbatim: sputtering machines are pretty cheap. They're like, like 800 to a thousand dollars approximately for the used ones.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: Direct-write rastering substitutes for mask-based exposure in a garage process, and that is precisely why such a setup cannot reach volume: a mask lets you print many chips in one exposure, and rastering does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: because you can't make a five nanometer mask and then, you know, do like a thousand chips at once
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor manufacturing is unusual in that the equipment is catalogue-purchasable: a would-be entrant can order machines from Applied Materials or Tokyo Electron, an option with no equivalent in, for example, resistor manufacturing.
claims.quote_verbatim: Applied materials or tell or whoever. And you could just go buy a, you know, a bunch of machines.
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: Atomic Semi was set up to build small, fast semiconductor fabs and to own the whole process from raw silicon upward, in reaction to the difficulty of buying the equipment and materials the industry depends on.
claims.quote_verbatim: Atomic Semi is building a small, fast semiconductor fab
claims.episode_title: The Magic of Calipers
